mechanisms.eyebrow: 当前位置 · 连续解说
mechanisms.scale: 机制示意，颗粒、距离与时间不按比例
mechanisms.density: 空气粒子越来越稀疏 · 点数仅作提示

layers.question: 云为什么常在靠近地面的空气里？
layers.lead: 地面是这段旅程的重要能量来源；抬升、冷却与水汽条件要一起看。

steps.title: 地面向空气传热
steps.body: 阳光先使地表受热；地表再把一部分能量传给邻近空气。

steps.title: 空气抬升并冷却
steps.body: 一团空气上升时周围气压降低，它膨胀，温度通常下降。

steps.title: 有足够水汽才可能成云
steps.body: 冷却到适当程度，水汽可凝结成小水滴或冰晶；水汽不够时没有这朵云。云滴还要继续长大才可能落雨。

layers.boundary: 两条路径分别示意水汽充足与不足；这里没有计算实时湿度、降雨量或天气预报。

layers.question: 为什么往上不再一直变冷？
layers.lead: 臭氧吸收一部分太阳紫外线，使平流层上部获得能量。

steps.title: 紫外线进入这一带
steps.body: 太阳的不同波段进入大气；这里特别追踪被臭氧吸收的部分紫外线。

steps.title: 臭氧吸收并使空气升温
steps.body: 吸收的辐射能量转成周围空气的热运动；平流层上部通常比下部暖。

steps.title: 上下翻动较难持续
steps.body: 这种温度结构通常抑制强对流，但仍有风和上下交换；臭氧不是一张挡住空气的薄膜。

layers.boundary: 光线与臭氧分子都放大了；吸收位置、比例和温度曲线不是现场测量。

layers.question: 天上的一道亮线从何而来？
layers.lead: 流星体高速进入空气；发光发生在飞行途中，并非固定在一条高度线上。

steps.title: 小天体从太空进入
steps.body: 画面追踪同一个流星体的来路；它与越来越多的空气相遇。

steps.title: 高速作用产生亮迹
steps.body: 气体被压缩、加热，流星体也会失去物质；发光的气体与物质留下短暂亮迹。

steps.title: 亮迹消退，结果未必相同
steps.body: 许多小流星体在高空消散；也有一部分碎片可能继续下落，最后成为陨石。

layers.boundary: 路径和亮度为示意；尺寸、速度与材料会改变结果，本页不预测某颗流星体是否落地。

layers.question: 空气稀薄，为什么还会有高温与极光？
layers.lead: 日光加热与极光是两条不同的能量途径，不能把高温当作极光的开关。

steps.title: 高能太阳辐射被吸收
steps.body: 一些高能紫外线与 X 射线把能量交给高层稀薄气体，使粒子的平均运动能量升高。

steps.title: 粒子温度高，空气仍很稀
steps.body: 单个粒子运动可很快，但粒子数量少；温度高不等于像地面热空气那样不断把大量热传给物体。

steps.title: 另在合适条件下出现极光
steps.body: 进入极区高层大气的带电粒子可使气体发光。没有相应粒子输入与磁场条件，不能只因这里温度高就画极光。

layers.boundary: 辐射、粒子与极光被放大；高层实际温度与极光位置随太阳和地磁活动变化。

layers.question: 空气究竟在哪里结束？
layers.lead: 越往外，粒子相遇越少；大气逐渐接上太空。

steps.title: 粒子相距很远
steps.body: 外逸层里粒子很稀疏，彼此碰撞比低空少得多。

steps.title: 有些仍留在地球附近
steps.body: 稀疏不等于都在飞走；一些粒子的运动仍受地球引力束缚。

steps.title: 有些轻粒子可以逃逸
steps.body: 足够快的轻粒子可能离开；其他粒子仍在更远处出现，没有一道整齐的终止墙。

layers.boundary: 1000 km 是本页观察上限，不是大气终点；虚线轨迹仅表示不同可能，不是实测轨道。

layers.name: 对流层
layers.story: 我们呼吸的空气、大多数云和天气，都在这层较低的大气里。向上走，空气通常越来越冷、越来越稀薄。
layers.science: 图中采用标准大气剖面作为比较基准，不是今天的天气。真实对流层顶随纬度、季节和天气变化，约 11 km 只是本图参考。地表向大气传热，但气温并非每处都单调下降，逆温也会出现。
layers.detail: 暖湿空气抬升、冷却，可以成云；云滴或冰晶长大后才可能降水。低云、高云与发展很高的雷雨云，大多仍在对流层。
layers.key: 弯箭头：抬升与下沉；横箭头：风。雨线只从示例雨云落下，不是每朵云都下雨。

layers.name: 平流层
layers.story: 再往上，温度变化开始不一样。臭氧吸收一部分太阳紫外线，使上方逐渐变暖。这里通常不容易发生强烈的上下混合。
layers.science: 稳定的垂直温度结构抑制强对流，但平流层不是禁止空气上下运动的硬壳。平流指输送过程，并非平流层专属。臭氧层也不是一层实体薄膜。
layers.detail: 臭氧吸收部分紫外线，上方逐渐变暖，强烈上下翻滚不容易持续；空气仍会水平输送。
layers.key: 紫色光线：部分紫外线被臭氧吸收。普通雨云很少来到这里；极冷的极地冬季可出现极地平流层云。

layers.name: 中间层
layers.story: 空气已经很稀薄，向上通常再次变冷。许多进入地球大气的流星体会在这一带产生可见的流星。
layers.science: 中间层顶高度和温度会变化。本图的干空气标准剖面只计算至约 85 km，不把它外推为真实高层大气。流星发光还取决于物体速度、组成和尺寸。
layers.detail: 向上再次变冷。小流星体高速进入空气，与气体作用，形成短暂的发光迹线，尾迹沿来路逐渐变淡。中间层顶附近在特殊条件下也可能有夜光云。
layers.key: 亮头标示正在强烈发光的位置，后方尾迹逐渐变淡；亮度、宽度和颜色是示意，不代表流星体大小。

layers.name: 热层
layers.story: 这里的粒子很少，但单个粒子可以有很高的运动能量。高温不等于像地面炉子一样把人烤热；空气太稀薄了。
layers.science: 热层温度和范围受太阳活动影响显著。这里不显示未经计算的温度和压力数值；高温描述粒子平均动能，物体热平衡还取决于辐射和粒子密度。国际空间站的轨道位于这一高度范围内。
layers.feature: 极光与稀疏的高速粒子
layers.detail: 这里空气很稀薄，粒子平均运动能量可以很高。在极区，一些进入高层大气的带电粒子把能量传给气体，气体随后放光，形成极光。温度高不等于到处有极光。
layers.key: 交叉小点：进入的带电粒子；空心圆：被放大的大气粒子；绿色光幕：气体发出的光。轨迹和颜色是教学编码，不是粒子真实形状或观测比例。

layers.name: 外逸层
layers.range: 约 600 km 以上，逐渐过渡
layers.story: 越往外，空气越稀薄，渐渐与太空相接。大气没有像墙壁一样突然结束的边缘。
layers.science: 外逸层下界随太阳活动等条件变化，600 km 仅为示意分界。图中 1000 km 是观察窗口的上限，不是地球大气的终点；100 km 常用作航天活动约定界线，也不代表上方没有气体。
layers.detail: 粒子之间相隔很远，一些轻气体粒子可以逃逸。继续往上仍可能有粒子，没有一堵“空气到此为止”的墙。
layers.key: 小点：稀疏粒子示意；不是可见尘埃，也不表示真实数量。

earth.name: 地球
earth.cloud: 云里主要是水滴或冰晶
earth.story: 水在空气、地面和地下之间迁移。先在熟悉的地球上找出空气与水的关系，再用同样的问题观察其他世界。

column.title: 逐渐接上太空
column.body: 空气越往外越稀薄，没有突然的边缘。

column.title: 臭氧与稀薄高空
column.body: 平流层里的臭氧吸收部分紫外线。

column.title: 水云与天气
column.body: 低空有风，水滴或冰晶组成云；有些云会降雨或雪。

column.title: 海洋与陆地
column.body: 液态水可以在地表汇成河流和海洋。

venus.name: 金星
venus.cloud: 厚云主要由硫酸液滴组成
venus.story: 金星与火星都以二氧化碳为主要大气成分，但大气量和地表环境非常不同。成分相似，不意味着压力和温度相同。

column.title: 逐渐接上太空
column.body: 云层上方仍有大气，往外逐渐稀薄。

column.title: 高空厚厚的硫酸云
column.body: 主要云层约在 45–70 km；云顶的风很快。

column.title: 云下：厚重、炎热的空气
column.body: 浓厚二氧化碳大气带来很高的地表压力；强温室效应使地表炽热。

column.title: 炽热的岩石地面
column.body: 没有地球那样的液态水海洋；不要把黄色云当成水雨云。

mars.name: 火星
mars.composition: 以二氧化碳为主，十分稀薄
mars.cloud: 可见水冰云，也有二氧化碳冰云
mars.story: 薄薄的大气和低气压，使火星地表的水与地球表现不同。图中的温度是代表均值，真实昼夜、纬度和季节差异很大。

column.title: 逐渐接上太空
column.body: 薄薄的大气继续向外延伸。

column.title: 高空也可以有冰云
column.body: 一些更高的云由二氧化碳冰组成，并非水云。

column.title: 稀薄空气、扬尘与水冰云
column.body: 风能卷起尘土；常见水冰云与高处二氧化碳冰云不同。

column.title: 寒冷、干燥的岩石地面
column.body: 地表气压远低于地球，没有今天地球式的常年露天液态水海洋。

titan.name: 土卫六
titan.cloud: 有甲烷云、雨及甲烷与乙烷湖海
titan.story: 土卫六是土星的卫星，不是行星。它很冷，地表液体循环主要涉及甲烷和乙烷；相似的循环形态不意味着流动的都是水。

column.title: 逐渐接上太空
column.body: 稠密大气向高处延伸，最终逐渐稀薄。

column.title: 橙色有机雾霾
column.body: 高空化学反应形成的微粒遮住地面；雾霾不是甲烷雨云。

column.title: 甲烷云与可能的甲烷雨
column.body: 这里很冷，甲烷可以凝结成云并降雨；并非处处、时时在下雨。

column.title: 冰质地面与湖海
column.body: 水冰像岩石一样坚硬；湖海里的液体主要是甲烷与乙烷。

moon.name: 月球
moon.composition: 几乎没有大气 · 极稀薄的外逸层
moon.cloud: 没有地球式的云、风与雨
moon.story: 月球是地球的卫星。少量气体粒子不等于一层能形成天气的空气；没有大气散射形成的蓝天，即使地面被太阳照亮，天空背景仍很黑。

column.title: 外部空间
column.body: 看不到像地球那样的厚空气层；少量气体粒子仍可存在。

column.title: 只有极稀薄的外逸层
column.body: 粒子非常分散，很少互相碰撞。这里不套用地球的五层结构。

column.title: 没有天气云和雨
column.body: 没有地球式的空气环流和降雨；亮着的地面上方也没有蓝天。

column.title: 直接露出的岩石地面
column.body: 遍布撞击坑。阳光照到和照不到的地方，表面温度可以差很多。

mercury.name: 水星
mercury.composition: 几乎没有大气 · 极稀薄的外逸层
mercury.cloud: 没有地球式的云、风与雨
mercury.story: 水星是一颗行星。它离太阳近，但没有厚大气来有效调节昼夜温度；面向太阳的地面很热，长夜中的地面很冷。太阳风是来自太阳的带电粒子流，不是这里的天气风。

column.title: 外部空间
column.body: 地面之外没有地球式的浓厚空气包围，只有极少的气体粒子。

column.title: 来自地表的少量粒子
column.body: 太阳风和微小撞击等过程会让一些原子离开地表，补充极稀薄的外逸层。

column.title: 没有遮住地面的雨云
column.body: 强烈日照可以直接照到地面；没有地球式的云雨系统搬运水。

column.title: 布满撞击坑的地面
column.body: 白昼炽热、夜晚很冷。这里的温度描述地表，不是能呼吸的空气温度。

diagram.title: 从地面向外，看空气在做什么
diagram.up: 向外 · 空气逐渐稀薄
diagram.ground: 同一片地面：海洋、陆地和我们
diagram.comparePrompt: 点选任一行，同时看两边的解释

highClouds.name: 平流层 · 极地平流层云
highClouds.body: 极地冬季极冷时才可能出现；不是普通雨云，也不是平流层每天都多云。

highClouds.name: 中间层顶附近 · 夜光云
highClouds.body: 高纬度夏季、极冷的高空可能出现薄薄冰晶云；不从这里给地面降雨。

energy.title: 极光的光从哪里来？
energy.intro: 把一次相互作用放大看：这不是三团不同的空气，而是同一个大气粒子先得到能量、再放出光。

steps.title: 带来能量
steps.body: 带电粒子进入稀薄的高层大气。

steps.title: 把能量传过去
steps.body: 碰撞使大气原子或分子进入激发态。

steps.title: 气体放光
steps.body: 激发态退回较低能态时，可以发出光。

energy.key: 交叉点＝带电粒子；圆圈＝大气粒子；波纹箭头＝发出的光。图形、间距与等待时间均不按实际比例；极光颜色还取决于气体种类和能量变化。

journey.projection: 黄色方框始终标记同一地面；亮点是观察高度 · 镜头从外侧观察，不是乘坐飞船 · 现象放大示意
journey.boundary: 球体与高度位置使用统一参考距离，镜头缩放会变化。远景采用地球参考贴图；靠近地面时保留同一标记，海岸细节转为教学示意，不是实测地形。云、箭头和粒子为放大示意；各类现象也不表示同时发生。
journey.overviewGuide: 先找到黄色标记，再拖动旅程或播放：地球会连续变大，标记附近的云和地面逐渐清楚。到达地面后，观察点再向上移动。
journey.question: 大气怎样包围地球，各层在哪里？
journey.story: 远看，大气贴着球体，像薄薄的边缘。我们先走近同一处海岸，再从低空的风和云向上，寻找臭氧、流星与极光所在的区域。黄色方框一直留在地面，不会跟着观察点升高。
journey.science: 采用半径 6371 km 的球形参考地球与正交侧视镜头。地表标记、各层高度和现象中心位于同一套径向坐标；镜头拉近与沿高度观察是展示路径，不是航天器动力学。低层读数仍使用标准大气参考。
journey.compare: 把地球与其他天空并排比较 →
journey.railNote: 各层展开示意，间距不按比例
journey.holding: 停一停，看看这里 · 3 秒后继续
clues: 从这处地面出发，抬头找云。
我们来到云的身边：下面仍是出发的海岸。
普通雨云已经在下面了；这里的臭氧吸收部分紫外线。
云和臭氧大多在下方；许多流星在这一带高空发光。
地面更远了；在合适条件下，这一带高空会出现极光。
回看下面：空气越来越稀薄，逐渐接上太空。

structure.scale: 地球各层分别展开，层内高度用对数映射；其他世界各用自己的窗口。地貌和现象另作放大，屏幕厚度不表示实际厚度或大气量。
structure.earthScale: 各层分别展开，层内高度用对数映射；横向与现象另作放大。分界是温度结构的参考位置，空气没有硬壳。
structure.context: 切开前侧，显露空气与地面的空间关系 · 教学重建
structure.choose: 选择现象，查看它在哪里
structure.noGpu: 三维画面不可用，仍可按现象阅读结构；可重试。
structure.air: 气体由浓到稀，连续过渡

weather.title: 对流层 · 水云与天气
weather.body: 低处空气较密，水汽多。湿空气抬升、充分冷却才可能成云，云滴还要长大才可能落雨。可选择晴空、有云无雨和降雨进行比较。
weather.visible: 云随风变化，有些云会下雨。
weather.clue: 空气抬升会冷却；水汽够多才可能成云，云滴还要长大才可能落雨。细线用来显示看不见的风。

ozone.title: 平流层 · 臭氧吸收
ozone.body: 臭氧吸收部分紫外线，使这一带上部通常更暖。上方淡紫光线逐渐淡去表示吸收；紫外线和臭氧本身都不是画面中肉眼可见的光。
ozone.visible: 客机从下方飞过；臭氧和紫外线都看不见，可用上方开关查看示意。
ozone.clue: 淡紫线向下逐渐变淡，表示部分紫外线被臭氧吸收、能量交给空气；这不是发光颗粒或飞机尾迹。客机示例约12 km，巡航高度与对流层顶都会变化。
ozone.reference: 客机示例约 12 km · 外形放大；巡航高度与对流层顶都因条件而异

meteor.title: 中间层 · 流星亮迹
meteor.body: 许多流星体在这一带与空气高速作用，失去物质并发光；亮迹跨越一段高度，结果随流星体而变。
meteor.visible: 同一个亮头划过高空，身后的亮迹逐渐消散。
meteor.clue: 流星体高速遇到空气，气体被加热，流星体也会失去物质；并非一条永久发亮的固体。

aurora.title: 热层 · 稀薄空气与极光
aurora.body: 空气已很稀薄。在适合的极区和粒子输入条件下，气体受激发光，形成有厚度和褶皱的极光帘。极光不由高温单独触发。
aurora.visible: 在合适条件下，极区夜空的光幕缓慢起伏，细光束忽明忽暗。
aurora.clue: 带电粒子沿磁场进入高空，使气体发光；关掉粒子输入作对照。高能日光加热是另一个过程。

escape.title: 外逸层 · 逐渐接上太空
escape.range: 约 600 km 以上 · 没有硬边缘
escape.body: 粒子碰撞很少，有些仍受地球引力约束，有些可以逃逸。画面的顶部只是观察窗口的边缘。
escape.visible: 稀薄高空几乎空无一物；一颗放大的低轨卫星提供位置参照。
escape.clue: 放大的点和轨迹表示少量粒子：有些仍被地球引力束缚，有些可以逃逸；它们不是可见小星星。 卫星仍受地球引力作用；不同任务的轨道高度不同。
escape.reference: 低轨卫星示例约 824 km · 外形放大，示例路径并非轨道计算

hot-ground.title: 炎热的岩石地面
hot-ground.body: 浓密大气下是炎热的岩石地面；剖面移开前侧空气与云，才看得到这里。地貌并非实测地点。
hot-ground.visible: 起伏的岩石地表，被浓厚空气与云幕笼罩。
hot-ground.clue: 暖色表示代表性照明和岩石，不代表整片地面是熔岩。

dense-air.title: 云下的浓密空气
dense-air.body: 金星近地空气远比地球浓密，地表压力约为地球的九十多倍。厚重的气体与温室效应一起影响地表环境。
dense-air.visible: 厚重的天空使远处地貌变得朦胧。
dense-air.clue: 颜色与透明度帮助区分金星的浓厚空气，不能按屏幕深浅读取密度。

acid-cloud.title: 连成云幕的硫酸云
acid-cloud.body: 大量微小硫酸液滴组成深厚云幕，遮住地表。这里是云层，并不与地球某一整层大气一一对应。
acid-cloud.visible: 厚云幕被高空的风带动，形状缓慢变化。
acid-cloud.clue: 云主要由微小硫酸液滴构成，不是地球水云；风迹放大显示高空流动，不表示地表同速。

venus-upper.title: 逐渐变稀的高空
venus-upper.range: 高层示例 · 不另定统一分界
venus-upper.body: 更高处气体逐渐变稀，太阳辐射也可使部分气体电离；它有自己的温度与电离结构。
venus-upper.visible: 云幕之上逐渐接近黑暗的太空。
venus-upper.clue: 点只提示高处仍有气体，不是地球热层与外逸层的一一对应。

dust.title: 稀薄空气里的风尘
dust.body: 火星大气以二氧化碳为主，地表压力不到地球的百分之一；风仍能扬起细尘，改变天空和地表。
dust.visible: 风在岩地上方带起尘土，地表仍看得见。
dust.clue: 尘点与风迹为了看清而放大；火星空气稀薄，这不是地球式雨云。

water-ice.title: 薄薄的水冰云
water-ice.range: 约 10–30 km · 一类低纬云的示例
water-ice.body: 火星也有水冰云。此处选择一类较低的薄云；云的实际高度随季节、地点和条件改变。
water-ice.visible: 薄薄的水冰云在高处缓慢变化。
water-ice.clue: 这是有条件出现的代表例子，不意味着这些云会向地面下液态水雨。

co2-ice.title: 更高处的二氧化碳冰云
co2-ice.range: 约 60–80 km · 暮光观测示例
co2-ice.body: 在很冷的高空，二氧化碳也能形成冰云。这些云和较低处的水冰云不是同一种物质，也并非总同时出现。
co2-ice.visible: 在暮光条件下，高处冰云仍能被太阳照亮。
co2-ice.clue: 这个例子是二氧化碳冰云，与较低的水冰云分开观察，不表示同地同时。

mars-upper.title: 稀薄高空与气体逃逸
mars-upper.body: 往外气体更稀薄，并与太阳输入相互作用；这幅图不把火星高空硬套成地球的五层。
mars-upper.visible: 稀薄天空继续向太空淡去。
mars-upper.clue: 放大点提示少量粒子，不给火星套上五层地球大气。

methane-lakes.title: 甲烷与乙烷的湖泊
methane-lakes.body: 土卫六的一些极区有液态甲烷、乙烷湖泊。这里的暗色液面不是水海，地貌是观察用的重建。
methane-lakes.visible: 低洼处是暗色的湖泊，岩岸与微弱反光能帮助辨认液面。
methane-lakes.clue: 湖中主要是甲烷、乙烷等液态烃，不是水；这里是湖岸示例，不是整颗卫星的表面。

methane-cloud.title: 有时出现的甲烷云
methane-cloud.body: 寒冷条件下，甲烷可凝结成云，并偶尔降雨。画面只展示一个有云的条件，不表示整颗卫星时时下雨。
methane-cloud.visible: 甲烷云会变化；选择下雨后，可以看见一次从云到地面的甲烷雨。
methane-cloud.clue: 这是偶发天气的例子，不把有机霾当成雨云，也不让所有云一直下雨。

organic-haze.title: 延伸到高空的有机霾
organic-haze.body: 阳光驱动氮气和甲烷参与化学反应，形成复杂有机物。细小霾粒造成橙褐色朦胧外观，和甲烷云分开。
organic-haze.visible: 橙色的霾层模糊了下方地表。
organic-haze.clue: 高空光化学过程形成有机气溶胶；它与较低的甲烷云是不同对象。

titan-upper.title: 更稀薄的上层气体
titan-upper.body: 霾与气体都随高度变化，空气逐渐接向太空；这里没有采用地球的臭氧层或极光层来补齐格子。
titan-upper.visible: 霾层上方仍有逐渐变稀的气体。
titan-upper.clue: 放大粒子只是位置线索；上缘不是一个真实的盖子。

moon-ground.title: 暴露的陨坑地表
moon-ground.body: 月面直接暴露在太空环境里；光照与阴影明显，没有地球那样的云雨。
moon-ground.visible: 陨坑边缘、岩石与阴影暴露在阳光下，没有云雨。
moon-ground.clue: 月球仍有极稀薄的外逸层；近真空不等于绝对没有粒子。

moon-exosphere.title: 极其稀薄的外逸层
moon-exosphere.range: 粒子被放大 · 非可见雾层
moon-exosphere.body: 月球仍有极少量气体粒子，碰撞很少。几个亮点只表示它们的存在，不代表真实粒径或数量。
moon-exosphere.visible: 肉眼看不到一层普通空气或雾。
moon-exosphere.clue: 放大的点表示相距很远的少量气体粒子，不是风吹起的尘云。

mercury-ground.title: 受阳光直照的岩石
mercury-ground.body: 水星是岩石行星。普通空气温度不能替代它随地点和昼夜强烈变化的地表温度。
mercury-ground.visible: 岩石、陨坑和强烈明暗差异清楚可见。
mercury-ground.clue: 地表温度随地点与昼夜强烈变化，不能用一个空气温度替代。

mercury-exosphere.title: 由地表补给的稀薄粒子
mercury-exosphere.body: 太阳风和微流星体撞击能使地表原子进入外逸层。这里不添加一层有天气的浓密空气。
mercury-exosphere.visible: 没有地球那样的云雨与厚重大气。
mercury-exosphere.clue: 地表释放的少量原子被放大为点；它们不是有天气的浓密空气。

structure.clueGuide: 云、雨、流星和极光是可观察现象；箭头、光线和大颗粒是解释线索。云雾形状、浓淡与速度经教学调整，不用于比较实测浓度或风速。
structure.weatherLabel: 对流层的一个天气例子
structure.focusNote: 近景突出当前现象 · 周围区域仍相连，现象分别放大
structure.earthContext: 高度虚线是温度结构的参考界限，会随条件变化；空气仍连续。

weatherVisible.dry: 阳光照着海湾和岩岸，空气在流动，这个例子没有形成云雨。
weatherVisible.cloud: 风推动云团，边缘逐渐变化；这里的云滴还没有长大到落雨。
weatherVisible.rain: 云随风移动，雨滴从云里显现、向下斜落，到达海面与坡地。

structure.shortScale: 高度与现象分别放大；窗口厚度不能直接比较，现象是不同条件的例子。

mechanismCues.label: 局部机制线索 · 非实测
weather: 暖色网格追踪水汽较多的气块，淡蓝网格表示较干的路径；背景云雨仍是独立天气示例。
同一气块向上、膨胀并冷却；观察它的位置和网格大小，不把它当成一颗水滴。
云在刚才湿气块的位置显现，较干路径没有这朵云；白云是小水滴或冰晶，水汽本身透明。
mechanismCues.dryWeather: 当前晴空例子只追踪较干路径：空气可以上升、冷却，但没有形成这朵云。
ozone: 先跟随淡紫色示意线进入臭氧较集中的区域；紫外线本身不可见。
线向下逐渐变淡，短的无定向暖色线表示能量交给空气，不表示强烈上升气流。
上部通常较暖，强烈上下翻动不易持续；水平细线仍显示空气可以输送。
thermosphere: 先看高能日光的能量进入稀薄空气；淡金线是不可见辐射的解释符号。
少量放大粒子的短线表示运动能量增加；粒子温度高不等于有大量热传给物体。
转看极区夜空的另一条路径：带电粒子先进入高空，气体随后发光；这不是高温自动变成极光。
mechanismCues.noAurora: 这次关掉了极区带电粒子输入：日光仍可加热稀薄空气，但没有这一路径产生的极光。

structure.compositionNote: 示意色分别增强，不比较占比或浓度
structure.compositionLimit: 成分示意层可单独开关：青色表示低层水汽的大致分布，淡紫色表示臭氧较集中的区域。两种颜色分别加强，不能比较成分占比；它们不是实测浓度，也不代表当前天气的湿度。水汽本身透明，白云是小水滴或冰晶，臭氧也不是紫色云壳。

mechanisms.scale: Mechanism illustration; particles, distances, and time are not to scale
mechanisms.density: Air particles grow sparser upward · dot counts are only a cue

layers.question: Why are clouds common near the ground?
layers.lead: The surface supplies much of the energy here; rising, cooling, and moisture must be considered together.

steps.title: The surface warms nearby air
steps.body: Sunlight warms the ground first; the ground transfers some energy to the air next to it.

steps.title: Rising air expands and cools
steps.body: As an air parcel rises, pressure around it falls. It expands, and its temperature usually drops.

steps.title: Enough moisture can make a cloud
steps.body: With sufficient cooling, water vapor can condense into droplets or ice. A drier parcel makes no cloud here; droplets must grow further before rain can fall.

layers.boundary: The two paths illustrate moist and drier air. This is not a calculation of live humidity, rainfall, or a weather forecast.

layers.question: Why does it stop getting colder all the way up?
layers.lead: Ozone absorbs some solar ultraviolet radiation, bringing energy to the upper stratosphere.

steps.title: Ultraviolet light enters
steps.body: Several wavelengths enter the atmosphere; here we follow the portion of ultraviolet light absorbed by ozone.

steps.title: Ozone absorbs energy
steps.body: Absorbed radiation adds energy to the surrounding air; the upper stratosphere is usually warmer than the lower part.

steps.title: Strong overturning is less likely
steps.body: This temperature pattern usually suppresses strong convection, but winds and vertical exchange continue. Ozone is not a solid film.

layers.boundary: Light rays and ozone molecules are enlarged; absorption position, fraction, and the temperature curve are not measurements here.

layers.question: Where does a bright meteor streak come from?
layers.lead: A meteoroid enters the air at high speed. Its glow follows part of a flight path, not a fixed height line.

steps.title: A small body arrives from space
steps.body: Follow one meteoroid along its incoming path as it meets more air.

steps.title: High-speed interaction makes a glow
steps.body: Gas is compressed and heated, and the body loses material. Luminous gas and material make a short-lived streak.

steps.title: The streak fades; outcomes differ
steps.body: Many small meteoroids disappear high up. Some fragments can continue downward and eventually become meteorites.

layers.boundary: The path and glow are illustrative. Size, speed, and material affect the outcome; this page does not predict whether one body reaches the ground.

layers.question: How can thin air have high temperatures and auroras?
layers.lead: Solar-radiation heating and auroras follow different energy paths. High temperature alone does not switch on an aurora.

steps.title: High-energy sunlight is absorbed
steps.body: Some extreme ultraviolet light and X-rays transfer energy to thin upper air, raising particles' average kinetic energy.

steps.title: Hot particles, very little air
steps.body: Individual particles can move rapidly, but they are few; high temperature does not mean continuous transfer of large amounts of heat like dense ground-level air.

steps.title: Auroras need other conditions
steps.body: Charged particles entering polar upper air can make gases glow. Without the relevant particle input and magnetic conditions, high temperature alone does not make an aurora.

layers.boundary: Radiation, particles, and auroral light are enlarged. Actual upper-air temperatures and aurora locations vary with solar and geomagnetic activity.

layers.question: Where does the air actually end?
layers.lead: Particles meet less often farther out; the atmosphere gradually blends into space.

steps.title: Particles are far apart
steps.body: Particles in the exosphere are sparse and collide much less often than they do low down.

steps.title: Some remain near Earth
steps.body: Sparse does not mean all particles are leaving. Earth's gravity still binds some of their paths.

steps.title: Some light particles escape
steps.body: Sufficiently fast light particles may leave; others occur farther out, with no tidy wall where the air ends.

layers.boundary: 1000 km is this page's viewing limit, not the atmosphere's end. Dashed paths show possibilities, not measured orbits.

layers.name: Troposphere
layers.story: The air we breathe, most clouds and most weather are in this low layer. Air usually becomes colder and thinner as we rise.
layers.science: The standard profile is a comparison reference, not today's weather. The tropopause varies with latitude, season and weather; 11 km is only this diagram's reference. Temperature inversions can interrupt the usual decrease with height.
layers.feature: A home for wind, clouds and rain
layers.detail: Moist air can cool as it rises and form clouds. Droplets or ice must grow before precipitation can fall. Low clouds, high clouds and tall storm clouds mostly remain in the troposphere.
layers.key: Curved arrows: rising and sinking air; horizontal arrows: wind. Rain falls only from the example rain cloud, not from every cloud.

layers.name: Stratosphere
layers.story: Higher up, the temperature trend changes. Ozone absorbs some solar ultraviolet radiation, warming the upper parts. Strong vertical mixing is usually suppressed.
layers.science: Stable stratification inhibits strong convection, but this is not a solid shell forbidding vertical motion. Advection is a transport process, not a process exclusive to this layer. The ozone layer is not a physical membrane.
layers.detail: Ozone absorbs some ultraviolet light, warming the upper part. Strong vertical overturning is inhibited, but air still travels horizontally.
layers.key: Violet rays: some UV absorbed by ozone. Ordinary rain clouds are rare here; polar stratospheric clouds can form in exceptionally cold polar winters.

layers.name: Mesosphere
layers.story: Air is very thin and usually cools again with height. Many incoming meteoroids produce visible meteors in this region.
layers.science: The mesopause height and temperature vary. The dry standard profile here stops near 85 km instead of being extrapolated into the upper atmosphere. Meteor emission also depends on speed, composition and size.
layers.detail: Temperature falls again. A small meteoroid enters at high speed and interacts with gas, producing a brief luminous streak that fades along its wake. Special conditions near the mesopause can also produce noctilucent clouds.
layers.key: The bright head marks strong emission; the wake fades behind it. Brightness, width and color are illustrative, not the size of the meteoroid.

layers.name: Thermosphere
layers.story: There are few particles, but each may move very energetically. High temperature does not mean heating you like an oven at ground level: the air is extremely sparse.
layers.science: Thermospheric temperature and extent respond strongly to solar activity. We do not invent numerical temperature or pressure readings here. Temperature describes particle kinetic energy; object heating also depends on radiation and density. The ISS orbits in this altitude range.
layers.detail: Air is very sparse, and its particles can have high average kinetic energy. In polar regions, some incoming charged particles transfer energy to atmospheric gas, which then emits auroral light. High temperature does not mean auroras everywhere.
layers.key: Crosses: incoming charged particles; outlined circles: enlarged atmospheric particles; green curtain: light emitted by gas. Paths and colors are teaching codes, not actual particle shapes or observed scale.

layers.name: Exosphere
layers.range: Above roughly 600 km, a gradual transition
layers.story: The atmosphere gradually becomes even thinner and blends into space. It does not end suddenly at a wall.
layers.science: The lower boundary varies with solar activity and other conditions; 600 km is illustrative. The 1000 km display limit is not the end of the atmosphere. The commonly used 100 km spaceflight boundary does not mean there is no gas above it.
layers.detail: Particles are far apart, and some light gas particles can escape. Gas can still exist farther out: there is no wall marking the end of air.
layers.trend: A gradual transition, not a shell
layers.key: Dots represent sparse particles, not visible dust or real particle counts.

earth.name: Earth
earth.cloud: Clouds mainly contain water droplets or ice
earth.story: Water moves between air, surface and underground stores. Establish the connection between air and water on Earth, then ask the same questions about other worlds.

column.title: Gradually into space
column.body: Air thins outward, without an abrupt edge.

column.title: Ozone and thin upper air
column.body: Stratospheric ozone absorbs some UV.

column.title: Water clouds and weather
column.body: Wind moves low air. Droplet or ice clouds sometimes bring rain or snow.

column.title: Oceans and land
column.body: Liquid water can collect in rivers and oceans.

venus.name: Venus
venus.cloud: Thick clouds mainly contain sulfuric-acid droplets
venus.story: Venus and Mars both have carbon-dioxide-dominated air, but vastly different atmospheric amounts and surface conditions. Similar composition does not mean similar pressure or temperature.

column.title: Gradually into space
column.body: Air continues above the clouds and thins outward.

column.title: High sulfuric-acid clouds
column.body: Main clouds lie roughly 45–70 km up; cloud-top winds are fast.

column.title: Below clouds: dense, hot air
column.body: Abundant CO₂ produces high surface pressure; a strong greenhouse effect heats the surface.

column.title: Extremely hot rock
column.body: No Earth-like liquid-water ocean. The yellow clouds are not water rain clouds.

mars.name: Mars
mars.cloud: Water-ice clouds and carbon-dioxide-ice clouds occur
mars.story: Thin air and low pressure make surface water behave differently from water on Earth. The temperature shown is representative: day, night, season and latitude differ widely.

column.title: Gradually into space
column.body: The thin atmosphere continues outward.

column.title: High ice clouds too
column.body: Some higher clouds contain CO₂ ice rather than water ice.

column.title: Thin air, dust and water-ice clouds
column.body: Winds lift dust. Water-ice clouds differ from higher CO₂-ice clouds.

column.title: Cold, dry rock
column.body: Surface pressure is far below Earth’s; no present-day Earth-like open liquid-water oceans.

titan.name: Titan
titan.cloud: Methane clouds and rain; methane–ethane lakes and seas
titan.story: Titan is a moon of Saturn, not a planet. Its very cold surface liquid cycle mainly involves methane and ethane. Similar-looking cycles do not mean that the liquid is water.

column.title: Gradually into space
column.body: A dense atmosphere extends upward, eventually thinning.

column.title: Orange organic haze
column.body: Particles formed by upper-air chemistry obscure the ground. Haze is not a methane rain cloud.

column.title: Methane clouds and possible rain
column.body: Cold conditions allow methane to condense and rain, but not everywhere or all the time.

column.title: Icy ground and lakes
column.body: Water ice is rock-hard. Lakes contain mainly liquid methane and ethane.

moon.name: Moon
moon.cloud: No Earth-like weather clouds, winds or rain
moon.story: The Moon is Earth’s satellite. A few gas particles do not make a weather-bearing atmosphere. Without a thick atmosphere to scatter sunlight into a blue sky, the sky background stays dark even over sunlit ground.

column.title: Outer space
column.body: No thick blanket of air like Earth’s; a few gas particles can still exist.

column.title: Only a tenuous exosphere
column.body: Particles are far apart and rarely collide. Earth’s five-layer structure does not apply.

column.title: No weather clouds or rain
column.body: No Earth-like air circulation or rain, and no blue sky over the sunlit ground.

column.title: Exposed rocky ground
column.body: Impact craters cover the surface. Sunlit and shaded surfaces can differ greatly in temperature.

mercury.name: Mercury
mercury.cloud: No Earth-like weather clouds, winds or rain
mercury.story: Mercury is a planet near the Sun. Without a thick atmosphere to redistribute heat effectively, sunlit ground gets very hot while the long nights get very cold. Solar wind is a flow of charged particles from the Sun, not local weather wind.
mercury.temperatureNote: Very hot days, very cold nights

column.title: Outer space
column.body: No dense Earth-like air surrounds the surface, only extremely sparse gas.

column.title: A few particles from the surface
column.body: Solar wind, small impacts and other processes release atoms from the surface into the tenuous exosphere.

column.title: No cover of rain clouds
column.body: Intense sunlight reaches the ground without an Earth-like cloud-and-rain system moving water.

column.title: Ground covered in craters
column.body: Very hot days and cold nights. These are surface conditions, not temperatures of breathable air.

diagram.title: From the ground outward: what is the air doing?
diagram.ground: The same ground: ocean, land and us
diagram.comparePrompt: Select a row to read both explanations together

highClouds.name: Stratosphere · polar stratospheric clouds
highClouds.body: Possible in exceptionally cold polar winters, not ordinary rain clouds or daily cloudy weather.

highClouds.name: Near the mesopause · noctilucent clouds
highClouds.body: Thin ice clouds can form in very cold high air during high-latitude summers. They do not bring rain to the ground.

energy.title: Where does auroral light come from?
energy.intro: An enlarged interaction: the same atmospheric particle gains energy and then emits light. These are not three different parcels of air.

steps.title: Energy arrives
steps.body: A charged particle enters the sparse upper atmosphere.

steps.title: Energy transfers
steps.body: A collision excites an atmospheric atom or molecule.

steps.title: Gas emits light
steps.body: Returning to a lower energy state can release light.

energy.key: Cross = charged particle; circle = atmospheric particle; wavy arrow = emitted light. Shapes, spacing and timing are not to scale. Auroral color also depends on the gas and the energy change.

journey.projection: The yellow square stays at the same surface site; the bright dot marks observation height · External camera, not a spacecraft ride · Features enlarged
journey.boundary: The globe and reference heights share distance coordinates as the camera zooms. The far view uses an Earth reference texture; near the surface, the same marker remains while coastal detail becomes a teaching illustration, not surveyed terrain. Clouds, arrows and particles are enlarged; the phenomena need not occur at the same time.
journey.overviewGuide: Find the yellow marker, then drag or play the journey. Earth grows continuously; clouds and ground near that marker come into view. After reaching the surface, the observation point moves upward.
journey.question: How does the atmosphere surround Earth, and where are its layers?
journey.story: From afar, the atmosphere hugs the globe as a thin rim. Approach the same coast, then move upward from low winds and clouds toward ozone, meteors and auroras. The yellow square stays on the ground rather than rising with the observation point.
journey.science: A reference spherical Earth of radius 6371 km is viewed with an orthographic external camera. The surface marker, layer heights and phenomenon centers share radial coordinates. Approach and ascent are a presentation path, not spacecraft dynamics. Lower readings remain a standard-atmosphere reference.
journey.compare: Compare Earth with other skies side by side →
journey.railNote: Layers expanded; spacing not to scale
clues: Start at this surface site and look up for clouds.
We are beside the clouds. Our starting coast is still below.
Ordinary rain clouds are below us. Ozone here absorbs some UV.
Most clouds and ozone are below. Many meteors glow at these heights.
The ground is farther away. Auroras can appear here under suitable conditions.
Look below: the air grows thinner and gradually meets space.

structure.guide: Drag to orbit · Scroll or pinch to zoom
structure.comparison: Each sky has its own structure
structure.scale: Earth regions are expanded separately with logarithmic height within each; other worlds retain their own windows. Terrain and phenomena are enlarged independently. Screen thickness is not physical thickness or atmospheric mass.
structure.earthScale: Regions are expanded separately with logarithmic height within each; width and phenomena are enlarged independently. Boundaries reference thermal structure, not hard shells.
structure.context: Foreground cut away to reveal air above ground · Teaching reconstruction
structure.choose: Select a phenomenon to locate it
structure.noGpu: 3D is unavailable. The phenomenon guide remains usable; you can retry.
structure.window: Top of observation window, not the atmosphere’s end

weather.title: Troposphere · water clouds and weather
weather.body: Low air is denser and holds most water vapour. Moist air can form clouds after sufficient lifting and cooling; droplets must grow before rain falls. Compare clear air, cloud without rain, and rain.
weather.visible: Clouds change with the wind; some bring rain.
weather.clue: Rising air cools. Enough water vapor can form clouds; droplets must grow before rain falls. Fine traces reveal invisible wind.

ozone.title: Stratosphere · ozone absorption
ozone.body: Ozone absorbs some ultraviolet radiation, usually warming the upper part. Fading violet rays above illustrate absorption; neither ultraviolet nor ozone is visible this way to our eyes.
ozone.visible: An airliner passes below. Ozone and ultraviolet are invisible; use the switches above to reveal explanatory guides.
ozone.clue: Downward violet lines fade as some ultraviolet is absorbed by ozone and transfers energy to air. They are explanatory marks, not glowing particles or an aircraft wake. The airliner is an example near 12 km; cruise altitude and tropopause height both vary.
ozone.reference: Airliner example: about 12 km · enlarged; cruise altitude and tropopause height both vary

meteor.title: Mesosphere · meteor trail
meteor.body: Many meteoroids lose material and produce light through high-speed interaction with air here. A trail spans heights and outcomes vary.
meteor.visible: One bright head crosses the upper sky; its wake gradually fades.
meteor.clue: A fast meteoroid heats the surrounding gas and loses material. The light is not a permanently glowing solid line.

aurora.title: Thermosphere · thin air and aurora
aurora.body: Air is very thin. With suitable polar location and incoming particles, excited gas emits a folded auroral curtain. High temperature alone does not cause aurora.
aurora.visible: Under suitable conditions, folded light slowly changes in the polar night sky.
aurora.clue: Charged particles follow the magnetic field into the upper air and make gas glow. Switch off their input for comparison. High-energy sunlight heats air through a separate process.

escape.title: Exosphere · gradual transition to space
escape.range: Above roughly 600 km · no hard edge
escape.body: Collisions are rare. Some particles remain gravitationally bound while others can escape. The top of this view is only an observation limit.
escape.visible: The sparse upper air looks almost empty. An enlarged low-orbit satellite gives a familiar reference.
escape.clue: Enlarged dots and paths represent sparse particles: some remain bound by gravity, others can escape. They are not visible stars. Gravity still acts on the satellite; orbit heights differ between missions.
escape.reference: Low-orbit example: about 824 km · enlarged; the illustrative path is not an orbit calculation

hot-ground.title: Hot rocky surface
hot-ground.body: Hot rock lies beneath the dense atmosphere. This cutaway removes foreground air and clouds to reveal it; the terrain is not a surveyed site.
hot-ground.visible: A rocky surface lies below thick air and clouds.
hot-ground.clue: Warm tones depict representative light and rock; they do not mean the whole surface is molten lava.

dense-air.title: Dense air below the clouds
dense-air.body: Near-surface air is far denser than Earth’s, with pressure over ninety times as high. The massive atmosphere and greenhouse effect shape surface conditions.
dense-air.visible: Distant terrain looks hazy beneath a thick sky.
dense-air.clue: Color and opacity distinguish the thick Venusian air; screen darkness is not a density reading.

acid-cloud.title: An extensive sulfuric-acid cloud deck
acid-cloud.body: Tiny sulfuric-acid droplets form a deep cloud deck that obscures the surface. This cloud deck is not a counterpart of one complete Earth atmospheric layer.
acid-cloud.visible: High winds carry a thick, slowly changing cloud deck.
acid-cloud.clue: The droplets are mainly sulfuric acid, not terrestrial water. Enlarged wind traces show high-altitude motion, not the same speed at the ground.

venus-upper.title: Thinning upper atmosphere
venus-upper.range: Upper region · no shared boundary imposed
venus-upper.body: Gas thins with height and solar radiation can ionise part of it. Venus has its own temperature and ionisation structure.
venus-upper.visible: Above the cloud deck, the sky gradually approaches dark space.
venus-upper.clue: Dots only indicate gas at high altitudes; these regions are not matched to Earth layer by layer.

dust.title: Windblown dust in thin air
dust.body: Mars has mostly carbon-dioxide air at less than one percent of Earth’s surface pressure. Wind can still lift fine dust and change the sky and ground.
dust.visible: Wind carries dust above the rocky surface, which remains visible.
dust.clue: Dust and wind guides are enlarged. Martian air is thin; this is not a terrestrial rain cloud.

water-ice.title: Thin water-ice clouds
water-ice.range: Roughly 10–30 km · one low-latitude cloud case
water-ice.body: Mars also has water-ice clouds. This is one lower, thin-cloud case; actual heights vary with season, place and conditions.
water-ice.visible: Thin water-ice clouds slowly change above the surface.
water-ice.clue: This is a conditional example, not a promise of liquid-water rain reaching the ground.

co2-ice.title: Higher carbon-dioxide ice clouds
co2-ice.range: Roughly 60–80 km · a twilight observation case
co2-ice.body: In very cold upper air, carbon dioxide can form ice clouds. They differ in material from the lower water-ice clouds and need not occur together.
co2-ice.visible: In twilight conditions, sunlight can still illuminate high ice clouds.
co2-ice.clue: This example is carbon-dioxide ice, shown separately from lower water-ice clouds; they need not coexist at one site and time.

mars-upper.title: Thin upper air and escape
mars-upper.body: Gas becomes still thinner outward and interacts with solar input. This view does not impose Earth’s five thermal layers on Mars.
mars-upper.visible: The thin sky fades toward space.
mars-upper.clue: Enlarged dots indicate sparse particles; Mars does not acquire the five Earth layers.

methane-lakes.title: Methane and ethane lakes
methane-lakes.body: Some polar regions of Titan have liquid methane and ethane lakes. The dark liquid is not a water ocean; terrain here is a teaching reconstruction.
methane-lakes.visible: Dark lakes occupy low areas; shores and faint reflections reveal the liquid surface.
methane-lakes.clue: The liquid is mainly methane, ethane and other hydrocarbons, not water. This is one lake-shore example, not the entire moon.

methane-cloud.title: Occasional methane clouds
methane-cloud.body: In cold conditions methane can condense into clouds and occasionally rain. This is a cloudy case, not continuous rain across the moon.
methane-cloud.visible: Methane clouds change. Select rain to observe a methane-rain example from cloud to surface.
methane-cloud.clue: This is occasional weather: organic haze is not a rain cloud, and not every cloud rains continuously.

organic-haze.title: Organic haze extending high above
organic-haze.range: Photochemical haze · not a hard shell
organic-haze.body: Sunlight drives chemistry involving nitrogen and methane, producing complex organics. Fine haze particles give a brown-orange veil distinct from methane clouds.
organic-haze.visible: Orange haze obscures the surface below.
organic-haze.clue: Upper-atmosphere photochemistry produces organic aerosols, distinct from lower methane clouds.

titan-upper.title: Thinner upper gas
titan-upper.body: Haze and gas vary with height as the atmosphere grades into space. Earth-style ozone and auroral regions are not added to fill a template.
titan-upper.visible: Above the haze, gas gradually becomes thinner.
titan-upper.clue: Enlarged particles are location guides; the top is not a real lid.

moon-ground.title: Exposed cratered ground
moon-ground.body: The lunar surface is exposed to space, with strong light and shadow and no Earth-like clouds or rain.
moon-ground.visible: Crater rims, rocks and shadows lie in sunlight, without clouds or rain.
moon-ground.clue: The Moon still has an extremely tenuous exosphere; near-vacuum is not literally zero particles.

moon-exosphere.title: An extremely tenuous exosphere
moon-exosphere.body: The Moon still has very sparse gas with rare collisions. Enlarged dots indicate its presence, not actual particle size or count.
moon-exosphere.visible: No ordinary layer of air or fog is visible.
moon-exosphere.clue: Enlarged dots represent widely separated gas particles, not a wind-blown dust cloud.

mercury-ground.title: Sunlit rocky ground
mercury-ground.body: Mercury is rocky. An ordinary air-temperature reading cannot stand in for its surface temperature, which varies strongly with place and day or night.
mercury-ground.visible: Rock, craters and strong light-and-shadow contrasts remain visible.
mercury-ground.clue: Surface temperature varies strongly with place and time of day; a single air temperature cannot replace it.

mercury-exosphere.title: Sparse particles supplied from the surface
mercury-exosphere.body: Solar wind and micrometeoroid impacts can release surface atoms into the exosphere. No dense, weather-bearing air layer is added.
mercury-exosphere.visible: There are no Earth-like clouds, rain or thick atmosphere.
mercury-exosphere.clue: A few atoms supplied by the surface are enlarged as dots; they do not form dense, weather-bearing air.

structure.clueGuide: Clouds, rain, meteors and auroras can be observed. Arrows, rays and enlarged particles are explanatory guides. Cloud/haze shape, opacity and speed are adjusted for teaching, not comparisons of measured concentration or wind speed.
structure.weatherLabel: One weather example in the troposphere
structure.focusNote: Close-up highlights this phenomenon · surrounding regions stay connected; phenomena are separately enlarged
structure.earthContext: Dashed heights mark variable thermal references; the air remains continuous.

weatherVisible.dry: Sunlight falls on the bay and rocky shore. Air moves, but this example forms no clouds or rain.
weatherVisible.cloud: Wind carries the clouds as their edges change. Droplets here have not grown enough to fall as rain.
weatherVisible.rain: Clouds move with the wind. Drops emerge within them, then fall at a slant to the water and hillside.

structure.shortScale: Height and phenomena are enlarged separately. Window thicknesses are not comparable; phenomena represent different conditions.

mechanismCues.label: Local mechanism guides · not measurements
weather: The warm wireframe follows a moister air parcel; pale blue marks the drier path. Background clouds and rain remain independent weather examples.
The same parcel rises, expands and cools. Follow its position and wireframe size; it is not a water droplet.
Cloud appears at the moist parcel's position; the drier path makes no such cloud. White clouds contain droplets or ice, while vapour is transparent.
mechanismCues.dryWeather: This clear-sky case follows only the drier path: air can rise and cool without forming this cloud.
ozone: Follow the violet guide into the ozone-rich region first. Ultraviolet radiation itself is invisible.
The ray fades downward; short, non-directed warm marks show energy transferred to air, not vigorous rising currents.
The upper region is usually warmer, limiting vigorous overturning. Fine horizontal guides still show that air can be transported.
thermosphere: First follow energetic sunlight entering sparse air. Pale gold guides stand for invisible radiation.
Short trails on a few enlarged particles indicate greater motion energy. High particle temperature does not mean a large heat transfer to an object.
Now view a different pathway in polar night: charged particles arrive first, then gas emits light. High temperature does not automatically create aurora.
mechanismCues.noAurora: Polar charged-particle input is off. Sunlight can still heat sparse air, but this auroral pathway produces no light.

structure.compositionNote: Colours enhanced separately; not fractions or concentrations
structure.compositionLimit: The composition overlay has its own switch. Cyan locates typical lower-air water vapour; violet locates the broad ozone-rich region. Each colour is independently enhanced, so they do not compare constituent fractions. They are not measured concentrations or the humidity of the selected weather case. Water vapour is transparent; white clouds contain droplets or ice. Ozone is not a violet cloud shell.
